title: False Weight
logline: A blacksmith's apprentice must retrieve a village relic stolen by raiders before the midwinter rite, or her mountain hamlet forfeits the protection three generations of iron have bought.
premise: A blacksmith's apprentice in a poor mountain village is sent to recover a relic raiders stole, because without it the midwinter rite fails and the village forfeits the protection it has paid for in iron for three generations. She is competent at her craft and at the hard practical work of retrieval, and she is bad at deciding what she owes the people who raised her. She recovers the relic and, reading it as a smith, finds it is a forgery. The forger is the master who raised her, who made it forty years ago for reasons that were good then and are not defensible now. She must choose what to do with that knowledge before the rite, and someone pays.

audience.reader_promise: A completed moral choice with a felt cost, a world that stays ordinary, and no last-page rescue.

places: the winter pass and the raider camp
the midwinter presentation ground below the valley Hold
rules_of_the_world: Magic exists only as binding: a named living person pays a concrete bodily or material cost; it never solves a plot problem without creating a worse one.
The midwinter rite is a compact with the valley Hold: present the village relic and the year's iron tithe, or forfeit one year of pass-protection and winter grain-right.
The Hold enforces the compact by closing the pass and withholding grain; it does not police the relic's inner authenticity unless the object is publicly challenged or broken.
A presentation-relic that is not the original holds the compact only while a living smith continues to pay a hidden levy bound into the piece at forging.
That levy cannot be transferred, paused, or discharged by any act available in this story except the bound smith's death or the relic's public breaking.
Ordinary metallurgy applies: heat, flux, weight, and quench behave as in a real forge; no metal is inherently magical.
The high passes in the three weeks before midwinter are traversable on foot but exact a physiological cost; the village can afford no mounts, guides, or shortcuts.
The village is too poor to buy a replacement relic, hire fighters, or meet a punitive extra tithe.
No prophecy, lineage-gift, or destined person exists; skill is taught and paid for in years of work.
Raiders are hungry people from poorer slopes, not an evil force; they steal because the Hold's protection does not cover them.

prose_touchstones: George Mackay Brown, rural chronicle prose
K. J. Parker workshop realism without the cynicism
spec-script format: slug line, action, cue, dialogue
forbidden_tics: prophetic cadence, portentous capitalization, or 'the old stories said'
weather used as cheap pathetic fallacy
invented glossary words for ordinary tools and places
interior monologue that names the theme
a closing sunset, snowfall, or thaw used as moral absolution
omniscient dips into any mind but the apprentice's
quest diction: chosen, destined, ancient evil, dark lord
camera directions (ANGLE ON, PUSH IN, WE SEE) and unfilmable interiority

suspense.intent: Keep the rite's deadline felt in weather and walking time, not in cuts or chases.

dread.intent: Winter and the compact's price should sit in the body, never as looming supernatural doom.

melancholy.intent: The forty-year kindness that became a lie should colour every shared task at the forge.

warmth.intent: Earn the cost of the break by showing real care in work taught and meals shared.

comedy.intent: Allow only dry craft remarks; never puncture the moral weight with wit.

awe.intent: Refuse wonder. Magic is a bill. Mountains are only mountains.

disgust.intent: Poverty should show in food, fuel, and bad iron, not in spectacle or gore.

catharsis.intent: The last choice must land in the body and the ledger, not as speech or sunrise.

realism_to_fantastication.intent: Stay in weather, weight, and work. The compact is felt as grain and closed passes.

interiority_to_exteriority.intent: Stay inside her craft-judgments and debt-confusion; do not leave her skull for other minds.

plot_to_character_driven.intent: The recovery clock forces choices; her failure at owing people decides which cost is paid.

dialogue_to_description.intent: Prefer the sound of the forge and the weight of a pack to talk that explains.

linearity.intent: Run almost straight from theft to rite; permit only brief work-memory, never a framed tale.

ambiguity_of_resolution.intent: We will know what she chose and what it cost; we will not know if she was right.

thriller.intent: Use only the rite-deadline as pressure. No pursuit set-pieces or last-second reveals.

romance.intent: No courtship. The bond is master and apprentice, parental and vocational only.

mystery.intent: The recovered object must be readable as wrong by craft knowledge before anyone confesses.

coming_of_age.intent: She is already a worker. This is a crossing in debt, not a blooming into self.

tragedy.intent: Someone pays a real price. No fall of a great person, no fated ruin.

satire.intent: Do not wink at the compact or caricature the Hold. Exploitation is ordinary.

adventure.intent: The retrieval is a hard walk and a theft, modest and physical, not a quest.

horror.intent: No uncanny dread. Bodies suffer from cold, work, and bargains already struck.

procedural.intent: Show how a smith reads metal and how a village stages a rite. Process is character.

war.intent: Raiders are a theft, not a campaign. Do not inflate them into an army.

domestic_drama.intent: The story lives in the forge-house: who taught whom, who lied, who still eats there.

moral_clarity.intent: Keep the old reasons intelligible and the present ones indefensible. No clean ledger.

institutional_critique.intent: The Hold's compact, not the raiders, is the structure that starves the village.

faith_transcendence.intent: The rite is a contract. Do not grant it holiness or a hidden grace.

class.intent: Iron, grain, and who walks the pass in winter should make the class relation visible.

gender.intent: Her being a woman at the anvil matters in who is sent and believed, not as a speech.

technology.intent: Craft knowledge is the only reliable power. It identifies the fake; it cannot unmake the cost.

must_include: recovery of the stolen relic before the midwinter rite
discovery that the relic is a forty-year-old forgery
the forger is the master who raised the apprentice
reasons for the forgery that were good then and are not defensible now
an exploitative protection-compact paid in iron, with the Hold as structural antagonist
two plots only, each constraining the other, with at least one because-link in each direction
the apprentice competent at craft and bad at deciding what she owes
an ending in which someone chooses and pays; neither triumph nor tragedy
must_avoid: prophecies, chosen ones, destiny, or bloodline gifts
ancient evil awakening or a Dark Lord
magic used as a solution to a plot problem
raiders as the sole or primary antagonist
a redemptive confession that restores the household without cost
a tragic annihilation of master, apprentice, or village
worldbuilding lectures and invented glossary words
omniscient dips, tense shifts, or a second POV
a third plot of any kind

keep_in_mind: Plant and pay off a motif of true weight versus false weight in metal, packs, tithe, and debt.
Pursuing the recovery must cost the relationship (time, trust, or the chance to hear him first); pursuing the relationship must cost the recovery or the rite.
Magic is a bill someone already pays. Never a key, never a spectacle, never a last-page out.
Do not redeem the master cheaply or damn him as simply selfish. The old reasons must still be audible.
Village poverty is structural: food, fuel, iron quality, and who can afford to walk the pass.
She thinks in work. Moral confusion should arrive as practical questions about what is owed, not as theme-statements.
Third person limited past, one narrator: the apprentice. No other interiority.
Below the exposé, no direct speech: reported semantics and illocutionary force only.
Prefer fewer, fully-discharged entities and events over scale. Honour plot_count = 2 exactly.
The Hold must remain an offstage or barely-seen institution; do not give it a villain face that replaces the system.
This is a SCREENPLAY. Scenes are rendered in spec format, roughly 70% dialogue to 30% action. Everything on the page must be photographable or audible; nothing may live only inside a head.
Because the medium is dialogue-led, state changes must land in what people say to each other or pointedly refuse to say. A change that happens only in narration cannot be filmed.
